claims.claim: Endogenous NCS1 may sequester its myristoylation motif to allow localization to cytoplasm.
claims.source: This result suggests that C-terminal tagging of NCS1 changes its localization potentially via exposing the myristoylation motif of NCS1, and endogenous NCS1 may sequester its myristoylation motif to allow localization to cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed localization patterns.

claims.claim: C-terminally LAP-tagged CEP15 localizes to the location between acetylated tubulin (a cilium marker) and Pericentrin (a centrosome marker), suggesting it localizes specifically to the mother centriole.
claims.source: Similar to NCS1, C-terminally LAP-tagged CEP15 localized to the location between acetylated tubulin, a cilium marker, and Pericentrin, a centrosome marker, suggesting that it also localizes specifically to the mother centriole (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: NCS1 localization to the mother centriole is enhanced upon serum deprivation.
claims.source: NCS1 localization to the mother centriole was enhanced upon serum deprivation (Figure 2C), a condition that induces cilium formation in RPE cells, much like several other distal appendage proteins (see Figure 1D of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Serum deprivation induces cilium formation in RPE cells.
claims.source: NCS1 localization to the mother centriole was enhanced upon serum deprivation (Figure 2C), a condition that induces cilium formation in RPE cells, much like several other distal appendage proteins (see Figure 1D of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about RPE cell behavior.

claims.claim: C-terminally LAP-tagged CEP15 localizes to a position slightly distal to the distal appendage protein, CEP164, in side view when observed via 3D-structured illumination microscopy.
claims.source: When observed via 3D-structured illumination microscopy with a resolution twice as high as a diffraction limited microscopy (Wu and Shroff, 2018), C-terminally LAP (EGFP-S)-tagged CEP15 localized to a position slightly distal to the distal appendage protein, CEP164, in side view (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: LAP-CEP15 forms a ring-like structure that is slightly smaller than the CEP164 ring when viewed from the top (axial view) of the mother centriole.
claims.source: When top (or axial) view of the mother centriole was visualized, LAP-CEP15 formed a ring-like structure that is slightly smaller than the CEP164 ring (Figure 2E), which mirrors the ninefold symmetrical structure of the distal appendage (Paintrand et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: NCS1 localizes slightly distal to CEP164.
claims.source: Similarly, NCS1 localized slightly distal to CEP164 (Figure 2F) as well as the binding partner, CEP89 (Figure 2G), and slightly proximal to the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34 (Stuck et al., 2021; Kanie et al., 2025; Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: NCS1 localizes slightly distal to CEP89.
claims.source: Similarly, NCS1 localized slightly distal to CEP164 (Figure 2F) as well as the binding partner, CEP89 (Figure 2G), and slightly proximal to the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34 (Stuck et al., 2021; Kanie et al., 2025; Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: NCS1 localizes slightly proximal to the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34.
claims.source: Similarly, NCS1 localized slightly distal to CEP164 (Figure 2F) as well as the binding partner, CEP89 (Figure 2G), and slightly proximal to the centriole-associated vesicle marker, RAB34 (Stuck et al., 2021; Kanie et al., 2025; Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2H and citations.

claims.claim: NCS1 forms a slightly smaller ring than CEP164 when viewed from the top of the mother centriole.
claims.source: Like CEP15, NCS1 formed a slightly smaller ring than CEP164 (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: The ring diameter of NCS1 is 319.5 ± 7.7 nm (n = 13, average ± SEM).
claims.source: Consistent with this, the ring diameter of NCS1 and CEP15 was 319.5 ± 7.7 nm (n = 13, average ± SEM) and 348.8 ± 8.0 nm (n = 16, average ± SEM), respectively (see Figure 1C of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data referenced in an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: The ring diameter of CEP15 is 348.8 ± 8.0 nm (n = 16, average ± SEM).
claims.source: Consistent with this, the ring diameter of NCS1 and CEP15 was 319.5 ± 7.7 nm (n = 13, average ± SEM) and 348.8 ± 8.0 nm (n = 16, average ± SEM), respectively (see Figure 1C of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data referenced in an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: Both CEP15 and NCS1 localize to the region close to subdistal appendage in some but not all centrioles.
claims.source: It is notable that both CEP15 and NCS1 also localized to the region close to subdistal appendage in some but not all centrioles (Figure 2D, F), consistent with what was observed for CEP89 localization (Chong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and 2F, and citation to Chong et al., 2020.

claims.claim: CEP15 was previously classified as a subdistal appendage protein.
claims.source: This near subdistal appendage localization explains why CEP15 was previously classified as a subdistal appendage protein (Gupta et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Centriolar localization of CEP89 is not affected by depletion of either NCS1 or CEP15.
claims.source: Centriolar localization of CEP89 was not affected by depletion of either NCS1 nor CEP15 (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: NCS1 fails to localize to the mother centriole in CEP89 knockout cells.
claims.source: NCS1 failed to localize to the mother centriole without altering its cytoplasmic localization in CEP89 knockout cells but not in CEP15 knockout cells (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), indicating that CEP89 recruits NCS1 to the distal appendage.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: NCS1 localizes to the mother centriole in CEP15 knockout cells.
claims.source: NCS1 failed to localize to the mother centriole without altering its cytoplasmic localization in CEP89 knockout cells but not in CEP15 knockout cells (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), indicating that CEP89 recruits NCS1 to the distal appendage.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The lack of NCS1 localization at the centriole in CEP89 knockout cells was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89.
claims.source: The lack of NCS1 localization at the centriole in CEP89 knockouts cells was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89 (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: CEP15 localization requires CEP89 but not NCS1.
claims.source: CEP15 localization required CEP89, but not NCS1 (Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2M and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Structural modeling using Alphafold2 shows that CEP89 interacts with both NCS1 and CEP15 whereas CEP15 does not interact with NCS1.
claims.source: This is further corroborated by the structural modeling using Alphafold2, which shows that CEP89 interacts with both NCS1 and CEP15 whereas CEP15 does not interact with NCS1 (Figure 2O; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 2O and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The expression level of neither NCS1 nor CEP15 is affected by CEP89 depletion.
claims.source: The expression level of neither NCS1 nor CEP15 was affected by CEP89 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D-E.

claims.claim: Both NCS1 and CEP15 are recruited to the distal appendage by CEP89.
claims.source: These results suggest that both NCS1 and CEP15 are recruited to the distal appendage by CEP89 (Figure 2N).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the localization dependency data.

claims.claim: The localization of other distal appendage proteins is unchanged in cells deficient in CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15.
claims.source: We also tested whether the three proteins affect localization of other distal appendage proteins and found that the localization of other distal appendage proteins were unchanged in cells deficient in CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C) (see also Figure 2A–L of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-C and referenced data.

claims.claim: NCS1 localization is greatly diminished in CEP83 or SCLT1 knockouts.
claims.source: Similar to the centriolar localization of CEP89, which was significantly reduced in CEP83 or SCLT1 knockouts, NCS1 localization was also greatly diminished in these knockouts (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claims.claim: CEP83-SCLT1 module serves as a structural component of the distal appendage.
claims.source: This is consistent with the observation that CEP83-SCLT1 module serves as a structural component of the distal appendage (see Kanie et al., 2025 for the detail).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: The feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2 is required for proper centriolar localization of NCS1.
claims.source: In contrast, the feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2 (see Kanie et al., 2025 for the detail) was required for proper centriolar localization of NCS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D) but not for CEP89 (Figure 2F of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D and referenced data.

claims.claim: The feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2 is not required for proper centriolar localization of CEP89.
claims.source: In contrast, the feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2 (see Kanie et al., 2025 for the detail) was required for proper centriolar localization of NCS1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D) but not for CEP89 (Figure 2F of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: CEP89 is a substrate of TTBK2.
claims.source: Given that CEP89 is a substrate of TTBK2 (Bernatik et al., 2020; Lo et al., 2019), this might suggest that phosphorylation of TTBK2 could affect the interaction between CEP89 and NCS1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bernatik et al., 2020 and Lo et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation by TTBK2 might affect the interaction between CEP89 and NCS1.
claims.source: Given that CEP89 is a substrate of TTBK2 (Bernatik et al., 2020; Lo et al., 2019), this might suggest that phosphorylation of TTBK2 could affect the interaction between CEP89 and NCS1.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known phosphorylation relationship.

claims.claim: NCS1 may be a phosphorylation target of TTBK2.
claims.source: It is also possible that NCS1 may be a phosphorylation target of TTBK2.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claims.claim: Control RPE cells form cilia over 24 hr after serum starvation, and almost all cells complete cilium formation between 24 and 48 hr.
claims.source: Control RPE cells form cilia over 24 hr after serum starvation, and almost of all cells completed cilium formation between 24 and 48 hr.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: CEP89 and NCS1 knockouts display a notable delay in initiating ciliation.
claims.source: CEP89 and NCS1 knockouts displayed a notable delay in initiating ciliation (see 12 hr in Figure 3A), but gradually catch up on ciliogenesis and exhibited only mild ciliary formation defects at later time points (see 48 hr in Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: CEP89 and NCS1 knockouts gradually catch up on ciliogenesis and exhibit only mild ciliary formation defects at later time points.
claims.source: CEP89 and NCS1 knockouts displayed a notable delay in initiating ciliation (see 12 hr in Figure 3A), but gradually catch up on ciliogenesis and exhibited only mild ciliary formation defects at later time points (see 48 hr in Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The cilium formation defect in CEP89 knockouts was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89.
claims.source: The cilium formation defect was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89 in CEP89 knockouts or untagged NCS1 in NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The cilium formation defect in NCS1 knockouts was rescued by expressing untagged NCS1.
claims.source: The cilium formation defect was rescued by expressing untagged CEP89 in CEP89 knockouts or untagged NCS1 in NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The kinetic defect in CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15 knockout cells is strongly consistent with the knockouts of several other distal appendage proteins, namely ANKRD26 and FBF1.
claims.source: This kinetic defect is strongly consistent with the knockouts of several other distal appendage proteins, namely ANKRD26 and FBF1 (Figure 5A, B of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: The ciliary length of CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15 knockout cells is comparable to that of control cells.
claims.source: The ciliary length of CEP89, NCS1, or CEP15 knockout cells was comparable to that of control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Ciliary ARL13B signal intensity is reduced in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts even after the cells complete cilium formation.
claims.source: Consistent with the cells deficient in ANKRD26 or FBF1 (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 of Kanie et al., 2025), ciliary ARL13B signal intensity was reduced in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts even after the cells complete cilium formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D and citation.

claims.claim: Even though NCS1 or CEP89 knockouts can eventually form primary cilia, those cilia may be functionally different from wild-type cilia.
claims.source: This suggests that even though the NCS1 or CEP89 knockouts can eventually form primary cilia, those cilia may be functionally different from wild-type cilia.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the reduced ARL13B signal in cilia of knockout cells.

claims.claim: CEP15 knockouts show similar but much milder kinetic defect of cilium formation than CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts.
claims.source: CEP15 knockouts showed similar but much milder kinetic defect of cilium formation than CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts, therefore, we focused on NCS1 in the subsequent investigation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: NCS1 knockouts exhibit moderate preciliary vesicle recruitment defect, similar to CEP89 knockouts, when assessed using RAB34 as the vesicle marker.
claims.source: Indeed, NCS1 knockouts exhibited moderate preciliary vesicle recruitment defect, similar to CEP89 knockouts, when assessed using RAB34 as the vesicle marker (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by vesicle recruitment assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Transmission electron microscopy analysis confirmed the vesicle recruitment defect in NCS1 knockouts.
claims.source: Transmission electron microscopy analysis confirmed the vesicle recruitment defect in NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3D, E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: The presence of fused vesicles in NCS1 knockouts suggests that NCS1 is important for recruitment but not fusion of the vesicle.
claims.source: The presence of fused vesicles, albeit much lower percentage than control cells, in NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3D, E) suggests that NCS1 is important for recruitment but not fusion of the vesicle.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of fused vesicles in NCS1 knockout cells.

claims.claim: Removal of CP110 is partially, but measurably affected in NCS1 knockout cells.
claims.source: Removal of CP110, which is believed to act as a cap of axonemal microtubule, was partially, but measurably affected in NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 3F), consistent with the fact that CP110 removal is in part downstream of the vesicle recruitment (Figure 4D of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CP110 removal assay data shown in Figure 3F and citation.

claims.claim: CP110 removal is in part downstream of the vesicle recruitment.
claims.source: Removal of CP110, which is believed to act as a cap of axonemal microtubule, was partially, but measurably affected in NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 3F), consistent with the fact that CP110 removal is in part downstream of the vesicle recruitment (Figure 4D of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: Neither IFT88 nor CEP19 recruitment to the centriole is affected in NCS1 knockout cells.
claims.source: Neither IFT88 nor CEP19 recruitment to the centriole was affected in NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 3G, H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claims.claim: NCS1 plays an important role in cilium formation by regulating preciliary vesicle recruitment, but not other known processes of cilium formation.
claims.source: These results suggest that NCS1 plays an important role in cilium formation by regulating preciliary vesicle recruitment, but not other known processes of cilium formation, consistent with the role of CEP89 in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing specific defects in vesicle recruitment but not IFT/CEP19 recruitment.

claims.claim: The distal appendage is indispensable for the recruitment of the preciliary vesicle to the mother centriole.
claims.source: As we showed in an accompanying paper, the distal appendage is indispensable for the recruitment of the preciliary vesicle to the mother centriole.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: Virtually no RAB34-positive ciliary vesicle is observed at mother centriole in cells deficient in CEP164, CEP83, or TTBK2.
claims.source: Virtually no RAB34-positive ciliary vesicle was observed at mother centriole in cells deficient in CEP164, CEP83, or TTBK2, which are critical for structural integrity of the distal appendage (Figure 5C of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: CEP164, CEP83, and TTBK2 are critical for structural integrity of the distal appendage.
claims.source: Virtually no RAB34-positive ciliary vesicle was observed at mother centriole in cells deficient in CEP164, CEP83, or TTBK2, which are critical for structural integrity of the distal appendage (Figure 5C of Kanie et al., 2025).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to data in an accompanying paper.

claims.claim: The vesicle recruitment phenotype in CEP164, CEP83, or TTBK2 knockouts is much stronger than what was observed in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts.
claims.source: This phenotype is much stronger than what we observed in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3C), suggesting that some other distal appendage proteins may compensate the lack of NCS1 for the preciliary vesicle recruitment.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the severity of phenotypes.

claims.claim: Some other distal appendage proteins may compensate for the lack of NCS1 in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
claims.source: This phenotype is much stronger than what we observed in CEP89 or NCS1 knockouts (Figure 3C), suggesting that some other distal appendage proteins may compensate the lack of NCS1 for the preciliary vesicle recruitment.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the partial phenotype in NCS1 knockouts.

claims.claim: Depletion of NCS1 decreases the percentage of ciliated cells in each single knockout cell line (FBF1, ANKRD26, KIZ, LRRC45, INPP5E), except CEP89.
claims.source: Cilium formation assay revealed that depletion of NCS1 decreased the percentage of ciliated cells in each single knockout cells, except CEP89 (Figure 4B, C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cilium formation assay data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claims.claim: CEP89, but no other distal appendage protein, regulates the same ciliary formation pathway as NCS1.
claims.source: This suggests that CEP89, but no other distal appendage protein regulates the same ciliary formation pathway as NCS1.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the double knockout data showing no additive effect for CEP89+NCS1 double knockout.

claims.claim: Depletion of NCS1 decreases the RAB34-positive centriole in each of the single distal appendage knockout cells, except CEP89 knockouts.
claims.source: Similarly, depletion of NCS1 decreased the RAB34-positive centriole in each of the single distal appendage knockout cells, except CEP89 knockouts (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by vesicle recruitment assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Yet unknown distal appendage proteins are required to compensate for the preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
claims.source: These results suggest that yet unknown distal appendage proteins would be required to compensate for the preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the partial phenotype and lack of complete epistasis with known proteins.

claims.claim: One or more integral components (CEP164, TTBK2, SCLT1, and CEP83) may be directly involved in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
claims.source: Another possibility is that one or more integral components (CEP164, TTBK2, SCLT1, and CEP83) may be directly involved in preciliary vesicle recruitment.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claims.claim: Myristoylation is required for membrane localization of NCS1.
claims.source: In contrast, NCS1-G2A was only found in the soluble fraction (15,000 × g supernatant) (Figure 5A), suggesting that myristoylation is required for membrane localization of NCS1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Membrane localization of CEP89 requires NCS1 with an intact myristoylation motif.
claims.source: Interestingly, CEP89 was only found in the soluble fraction (15,000 × g supernatant) in NCS1 knockout cells expressing either empty vector or NCS1-G2A, but not NCS1-WT. This suggests that membrane localization of CEP89 requires NCS1 with an intact myristoylation motif.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Both wild-type and the myristoylation defective (G2A) NCS1 localize to the mother centriole to a similar extent when expressed at similar level to endogenous NCS1.
claims.source: When expressed at similar level to endogenous NCS1 (Figure 5B), both wild-type and the myristoylation defective (G2A) NCS1 localizes to the mother centriole to a similar extent (Figure 5C, D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C-D and expression data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The myristoylation defective mutant of NCS1 almost completely fails to rescue ciliation defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
claims.source: However, the myristoylation defective mutant almost completely failed to rescue ciliation and preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 5E, F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The myristoylation defective mutant of NCS1 almost completely fails to rescue preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells.
claims.source: However, the myristoylation defective mutant almost completely failed to rescue ciliation and preciliary vesicle recruitment defect of NCS1 knockout cells (Figure 5E, F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: NCS1 recruits preciliary vesicle to the distal appendage via its myristoylation motif.
claims.source: These data suggest that NCS1 recruits preciliary vesicle to the distal appendage via its myristoylation motif.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing myristoylation is required for function but not localization.

claims.claim: The three intact Ca2+-binding EF hands and the Gly2 myristoylation site of NCS1 cluster on one face, while the CEP89-binding pocket occupies the opposite face.
claims.source: Structural modeling of the NCS1–CEP89 complex reveals a distinct functional organization of NCS1 (Figure 5G). The three intact Ca2+-binding EF hands and the Gly2 myristoylation site cluster on one face of NCS1, while the CEP89-binding pocket occupies the opposite face.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The arrangement of NCS1 functional domains suggests that NCS1 can simultaneously engage in membrane association and calcium sensing while interacting with CEP89.
claims.source: This arrangement suggests that NCS1 can simultaneously engage in membrane association and calcium sensing while interacting with CEP89.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural model showing spatial separation of functional domains.

claims.claim: Human NCS1 has three functional and one apparently non-functional EF-hand motif.
claims.source: In addition to myristoylation motif, human NCS1 also has three functional and one apparently non-functional (due to the mutation in critical amino acids needed for co-ordination bond with calcium) EF-hand motifs (Bourne et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bourne et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Several other NCS family proteins, including Recoverin and Hippocalcin, show a calcium-myristoyl switch.
claims.source: Several other NCS family proteins, including Recoverin and Hippocalcin, show a calcium-myristoyl switch (Ames et al., 1997; O'Callaghan et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ames et al., 1997 and O'Callaghan et al., 2003.

claims.claim: It has been proposed that NCS1 may employ a calcium-myristoyl switch similar to other NCS family proteins.
claims.source: In this mechanism, the sequestered myristoylation motif is exposed to allow the protein to bind membrane upon calcium binding. It has been proposed that NCS1 may employ a similar molecular switch.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a hypothesis in the field.

claims.claim: The structure of fission yeast Ncs1 solved by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed the calcium-myristoyl switch.
claims.source: While the structure of fission yeast Ncs1, solved by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed the calcium-myristoyl switch (Lim et al., 2011), several lines of evidence suggest the absence of that type of switch in budding yeast and mammalian NCS1 (Ames et al., 2000; O'Callaghan et al., 2002; Lemire et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Several lines of evidence suggest the absence of calcium-myristoyl switch in budding yeast and mammalian NCS1.
claims.source: While the structure of fission yeast Ncs1, solved by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed the calcium-myristoyl switch (Lim et al., 2011), several lines of evidence suggest the absence of that type of switch in budding yeast and mammalian NCS1 (Ames et al., 2000; O'Callaghan et al., 2002; Lemire et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ames et al., 2000; O'Callaghan et al., 2002; and Lemire et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The E84Q mutant of NCS1 as well as any double and triple EF-hand mutants are highly destabilized.
claims.source: The E84Q mutant as well as any double and triple EF-hand mutants were highly destabilized (see input in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and the centriolar NCS1 signal intensity of the mutants was reduced in parallel to their diminished expression level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The first EF hand is indispensable for stability of NCS1.
claims.source: This suggests that the first EF hand is indispensable for stability of NCS1.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the destabilization of E84Q mutant.

claims.claim: The E120Q mutant of NCS1 has similar expression level to wild-type, but its centrosomal signal is significantly reduced.
claims.source: E120Q mutant had similar expression level, but its centrosomal signal was significantly reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), consistent with its diminished interaction with CEP89 (see IP: GFP in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), a protein that recruits NCS1 to the mother centriole (Figure 2L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: The second EF hand is involved in keeping the structure of NCS1 to interact with CEP89.
claims.source: This suggests that the second EF hand is involved in keeping its structure to interact with CEP89.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced CEP89 binding of E120Q mutant.

claims.claim: The E168Q mutation has a negligible effect on stability and localization of NCS1.

results.result: NCS1 is identified as a stoichiometric interactor of CEP89 through tandem affinity purification and mass spectrometry, with direct binding confirmed by in vitro assays. The N-terminal region (1-343 a.a.) of CEP89 is required for NCS1 binding, and CEP89 serves to bridge NCS1 and CEP15.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35, and C38 provide converging evidence from TAP-MS, co-immunoprecipitation, and in vitro binding assays demonstrating the NCS1-CEP89 interaction. Claims C46 and C49 map the binding interface, and C51 establishes the bridging function. The data are internally consistent and supported by multiple orthogonal methods.

results.result: NCS1 localizes to the distal appendage at a position between CEP89 and the vesicle marker RAB34, forming a ring structure slightly smaller than CEP164 with a diameter of 319.5 ± 7.7 nm.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C67-C70 provide super-resolution microscopy data showing NCS1's precise spatial positioning relative to known distal appendage markers. Claims C71-C72 provide quantitative measurements of ring diameters. The localization data are consistent across multiple markers and imaging modalities.

results.result: CEP89 recruits NCS1 to the distal appendage, as demonstrated by complete loss of NCS1 centriolar localization in CEP89 knockout cells and rescue by CEP89 re-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C76 show loss of NCS1 localization in CEP89 knockouts, C78 demonstrates rescue, and C82 synthesizes the recruitment hierarchy. The genetic epistasis data strongly support the recruitment model, though the mechanism of recruitment remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: NCS1 knockout cells exhibit defects in preciliary vesicle recruitment and cilium formation, with a notable delay in initiating ciliation that is partially rescued over time. The defects are specific to vesicle recruitment, not vesicle fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C92-C93 establish the kinetic ciliation defect with quantitative data from Figure 3A. Claims C94-C95 demonstrate genetic rescue. Claims C101-C103 provide mechanistic insight through vesicle recruitment assays and electron microscopy. The presence of fused vesicles in knockouts (C103) supports the specificity for recruitment over fusion.

results.result: NCS1 recruits preciliary vesicles via its myristoylation motif. The myristoylation-defective G2A mutant localizes normally to the centriole but fails to rescue vesicle recruitment and ciliation defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 establish myristoylation's role in membrane localization through fractionation. Claims C120-C122 demonstrate the critical separation of localization from function: G2A localizes but cannot rescue. Claim C123 synthesizes the mechanism. This is a key mechanistic insight supported by multiple complementary experiments in Figure 5.

results.result: Double knockout analysis reveals that CEP89 and NCS1 function in the same pathway for cilium formation and vesicle recruitment, while other distal appendage proteins (FBF1, ANKRD26, KIZ, LRRC45, INPP5E) show additive defects with NCS1 depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C113 and C115 provide epistasis data from double knockout experiments showing no additive effect for CEP89+NCS1 but additive effects for other proteins. Claim C114 correctly infers pathway relationships. The genetic logic is sound, though the interpretation assumes complete loss of function in single knockouts.

results.result: NCS1 traffics to the distal appendage by microtubule-independent mechanisms (possibly diffusion), while preciliary vesicles require microtubule-dependent transport. NCS1 localization is independent of vesicle presence.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C142 establish microtubule dependence of vesicle recruitment through nocodazole treatment. Claims C143-C144 show NCS1 accumulation despite nocodazole. Claims C146-C147 demonstrate independence from vesicles using RAB34 knockouts. The data support distinct trafficking mechanisms, though the diffusion model (C144) remains speculative.

results.result: NCS1 is expressed in a wide range of murine tissues and localizes to the ciliary base in both neuronal and non-neuronal ciliated cells, with the notable exception of photoreceptor cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C154 provide comprehensive tissue expression and localization data from immunoblots and immunofluorescence across multiple cell types. Claim C153 validates antibody specificity using knockouts. Claim C155 identifies photoreceptors as an exception. The data are extensive and well-controlled.

results.result: Ncs1 knockout causes modest cilium formation defects in MEFs and reduced ciliary ARL13B signal, but no measurable ciliation defect in hippocampal neurons despite decreased ciliary ADCY3 signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C157 show MEF phenotypes, while C158-C159 show differential effects in neurons. The data suggest cell-type-specific requirements for NCS1, though the lack of neuronal ciliation defect (C158) may reflect technical limitations in assessing neuronal ciliogenesis kinetics as discussed by the authors.

results.result: Ncs1−/− mice exhibit obesity starting at 9-10 weeks with increased fat accumulation but do not show preweaning lethality or other common ciliopathy phenotypes (retinal degeneration, polycystic kidney, male infertility).
results.evaluation: Claims C160 and C162 establish the obesity phenotype with quantitative body weight data. Claim C165 demonstrates increased fat mass. Claims C167-C169 document absence of other ciliopathy phenotypes. The phenotypic characterization is thorough, though the discrepancy with previous studies (C160) regarding lethality suggests strain-specific effects.

results.result: NCS1 regulates preciliary vesicle recruitment but not other cilium formation processes: CP110 removal is partially affected (downstream of vesicle recruitment), while IFT88 and CEP19 recruitment are unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C104 and C106 provide quantitative data showing selective effects on CP110 but not IFT88/CEP19. Claim C105 contextualizes CP110 as downstream of vesicle recruitment. Claim C107 synthesizes the specificity. The data support a specific role in vesicle recruitment rather than general ciliogenesis defects.

results.result: Structural modeling reveals functional organization of NCS1 with Ca2+-binding sites and myristoylation motif on one face and CEP89-binding pocket on the opposite face, allowing simultaneous membrane association, calcium sensing, and CEP89 interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C124 and C47 describe AlphaFold2 structural predictions showing spatial organization. Claim C125 infers functional implications. Claim C80 extends to the pentameric complex. While computational predictions require experimental validation, they are consistent with functional data and provide mechanistic insight.

results.result: EF-hand mutations reveal that calcium binding is primarily required for NCS1 structure and stability rather than a calcium-myristoyl switch. The first EF-hand is critical for stability, the second for CEP89 interaction, while single EF-hand mutants retain function.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C137 provide systematic mutagenesis data showing differential effects of EF-hand mutations on stability, localization, and function. Claims C138-C139 correctly interpret the absence of a calcium-myristoyl switch. The data argue against a regulatory switch model and support a structural role for calcium.

results.result: N-terminal and C-terminal tagging of NCS1 produce different localization patterns: N-terminal tags preserve cytoplasmic/centriolar localization while C-terminal tags cause membrane localization, suggesting C-terminal tagging exposes the myristoylation motif.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 document differential localization with systematic tagging experiments. Claims C60-C61 provide mechanistic interpretation. The data are internally consistent and explain discrepancies with prior literature (C55), though the sequestration model (C61) remains speculative.

results.result: Localization hierarchy analysis reveals CEP89 is upstream of both NCS1 and CEP15, with CEP89 localization independent of NCS1/CEP15, while NCS1 and CEP15 require CEP89 but not each other. Other distal appendage proteins are unaffected by CEP89/NCS1/CEP15 depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C75, C77, and C79 establish the localization hierarchy through systematic knockout analysis. Claims C81 and C83 rule out indirect effects through protein stability or other distal appendage proteins. The genetic epistasis is clear and well-controlled.

results.result: NCS1 localization requires the structural components CEP83-SCLT1 and the feedback complex CEP164-TTBK2, while CEP89 localization requires CEP83-SCLT1 but not CEP164-TTBK2.
results.evaluation: Claims C84 and C86 provide localization data in various knockout backgrounds. Claims C85 and C87 contextualize with references to the accompanying paper. The data reveal differential requirements suggesting NCS1 recruitment may be regulated by TTBK2 phosphorylation.

results.result: CEP89, NCS1, and CEP15 knockout cells form cilia of normal length but with reduced ciliary ARL13B signal intensity, suggesting functional differences from wild-type cilia despite eventual cilium formation.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 establishes normal cilium length, C98 shows reduced ARL13B signal, and C99 infers functional consequences. The data suggest quantitative rather than qualitative defects in cilia, though the functional significance of reduced ARL13B requires further investigation.

results.result: CEP15 does not directly bind NCS1 in vitro, establishing that CEP89 bridges the two proteins rather than forming a direct NCS1-CEP15 interaction.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 provides negative binding data from in vitro assays, and C51 correctly infers the bridging model. The negative result is important for establishing the protein complex architecture and is consistent with localization dependencies.

results.result: NCS1 localization to the mother centriole is enhanced upon serum deprivation, a condition that induces cilium formation in RPE cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 provides quantitative data from Figure 2C showing enhanced localization. Claim C64 establishes the biological context. The data are consistent with NCS1's role in ciliogenesis, though the mechanism of enhanced recruitment is not addressed.

results.result: CEP89 lacks a membrane-binding motif, leading to the hypothesis that an interacting partner may directly bind preciliary vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claim C2 states the absence of membrane-binding motifs based on sequence analysis. Claim C34 presents the logical hypothesis that motivated the search for NCS1. This represents sound reasoning that led to the key discovery, though the initial observation is based on bioinformatic inference.

results.result: The partial vesicle recruitment defect in NCS1 knockouts suggests compensation by yet-unknown distal appendage proteins or direct involvement of integral components (CEP164, TTBK2, SCLT1, CEP83).
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C116, and C117 are speculative hypotheses to explain the partial phenotype. While the reasoning is sound, these remain untested possibilities requiring future investigation. The speculation is appropriately qualified but does not constitute a supported result.

results.result: TTBK2 phosphorylation might affect the CEP89-NCS1 interaction, and NCS1 may be a phosphorylation target of TTBK2.
results.evaluation: Claims C89 and C90 are speculative hypotheses based on known CEP89 phosphorylation by TTBK2 (C88) and the requirement for TTBK2 in NCS1 localization (C86). These are reasonable hypotheses but lack experimental support and are appropriately presented as speculation.

results.result: NCS1 is unlikely to use the UNC119 pathway for trafficking to the distal appendage based on absence from mass spectrometry data.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 is based on negative evidence from AP-MS and published UNC119 interactomes. While negative data have limitations, the conclusion is reasonable given the comprehensive mass spectrometry analysis and is appropriately qualified as "unlikely" rather than definitively ruled out.

results.result: The difference in preweaning lethality between this study and previous studies might derive from mouse strain background differences (C57BL/6J vs C57BL/6N).
results.evaluation: Claim C161 is speculation about the source of phenotypic discrepancies with prior studies. While strain differences are a plausible explanation, this remains untested. The authors appropriately present this as a possibility rather than a conclusion.

results.result: The obesity phenotype in Ncs1−/− mice is consistent with previous reports and similar to cilia-defective mice, potentially reflecting ciliary defects. The absence of retinal degeneration may reflect lack of NCS1 at the photoreceptor ciliary base, and the milder overall phenotype may reflect modest cilium formation defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C164 establish consistency with prior literature through citations. Claims C166, C170, and C171 provide reasonable mechanistic interpretations linking phenotypes to ciliary function and NCS1 localization patterns. The inferences are logical though causality is not definitively established.

results.result: Background claims establishing the known biology of primary cilia, cilium formation pathways, and the distal appendage structure and function.
results.evaluation: These claims (C11-C32) represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. They provide necessary context for the study but do not constitute novel findings. The citations appear accurate based on the references provided.

results.result: Background claims about NCS1 protein family characteristics, prior functional studies, and calcium-myristoyl switch mechanisms in related proteins.
results.evaluation: These claims (C39-C45, C126-C130, C140) represent prior knowledge about NCS1 and related proteins, appropriately cited. They establish the state of the field and provide context for the mechanistic studies. The literature citations appear accurate.

results.result: Background claims about CEP89 function and distal appendage requirements from the accompanying paper.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C33, C108-C110) reference findings from the accompanying paper (Kanie et al., 2025). While we cannot fully evaluate the accompanying paper, these claims provide necessary context and are appropriately cited. The cross-referencing between companion papers is appropriate.

results.result: Technical and nomenclature claims including CEP15 renaming, protein domain mapping, and localization details.
results.evaluation: These claims provide technical details about protein nomenclature (C37), domain requirements (C48), and detailed localization patterns (C62, C65-C66, C73-C74). The data are supported by the referenced figures and are consistent with the overall findings.

results.result: Comparative claims establishing consistency with other distal appendage proteins and prior studies.
results.evaluation: These claims (C36, C96, C100, C105) establish consistency with prior literature and the accompanying paper. They provide important context showing that NCS1/CEP89 phenotypes are similar to other distal appendage proteins, supporting the biological significance of the findings.
